summary: Lists the requirements for a protocol that sets up the security keys for encrypted SIP media streams (SRTP). Beyond basic security needs, such a protocol must work smoothly with SIP. It also summarizes and compares the proposals that existed at the time.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people on a SIP call, the protocol used to place internet phone calls, must agree on a secret key before they can encrypt their voice. This RFC lists what that agreement has to cope with, from calls forwarded to another person to attackers who listen in, and compares the key exchange methods that existed when it was written.

subtitle: What a protocol that agrees on SRTP encryption keys must handle, and how the keying methods of 2009 measured up.

tldr.problem: Two parties on a SIP call cannot encrypt their media with SRTP until they agree on the same cryptographic keys, and the everyday patterns of SIP calls make that agreement awkward.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements under an R- prefix, split into the key management protocol itself, the attack scenarios it must resist, and needs that can be met elsewhere in the system.
tldr.outcome: No protocol is specified. The document gives designers a checklist and a table comparing the keying mechanisms that existed in 2009, among them MIKEY, ZRTP and DTLS-SRTP.

today: RFC 5479 is an Informational memo published in April 2009, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a requirements document rather than a protocol, so there is nothing in it to implement on its own; it remains a checklist and a comparison table of the keying mechanisms that were available at the time.

sections.title: What This RFC Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
RFC 5479 collects requirements for a protocol that negotiates the cryptographic keys and parameters used by Secure RTP (SRTP), the encryption layer for media carried over RTP. It does not specify a protocol of its own. Instead it names what such a protocol must do, and it reviews the proposals that existed when it was written.

The work started when SIP, the protocol used to set up internet phone calls, was still young. As SIP deployments grew and new extensions and related protocols appeared, the need for end-to-end media security was re-examined. Re-reading an earlier design against the needs real users have is a normal way to check that the result still fits.

The document is organised in three parts. Section 3 describes the attacks a key exchange must resist, Section 4 walks through the call scenarios that cause trouble, and Section 5 lists the requirements themselves. Appendix A compares the existing keying mechanisms against those scenarios and against the security criteria, and Appendix B lists the questions the document deliberately leaves out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC does not build a protocol. It sets out a checklist for one: what an attack must look like before media can be decrypted, and which real call situations the key exchange has to survive.

sections.title: Signaling Path, Media Path and Adversaries
sections.content:
The RFC splits a call into two paths. The signaling path is the route taken by the SIP messages exchanged between the calling and called user agents, usually through SIP proxy servers. The media path is the route taken by the media packets. In the simplest case the two endpoints exchange media directly, and the media path is defined by a quartet of IP addresses and TCP or UDP ports plus an IP route; in other cases it also includes RTP relays, mixers, transcoders, session border controllers, NATs or media gateways.

An adversary is passive if it can learn information from the traffic but cannot alter it, and active if it can alter it. Three further terms matter. An Address-of-Record (AOR) is the public SIP or SIPS address of a user, which a location service maps to an address where the user might be found. The SSRC is the 32-bit value in RTP that identifies the synchronization source. A two-time pad is the use of the same key and the same keystream to encrypt different data, which in SRTP happens when two senders use the same key and the same RTP SSRC value. Perfect forward secrecy means that disclosure of the long-term secret keying material does not compromise the secrecy of keys agreed in earlier runs.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC splits a call in two: the messages that set it up, and the media that carries the sound. It also sorts attackers into those who only listen and those who can also change what they hear.

sections.title: Attack Scenarios and the Robustness Classes
sections.content:
The RFC classifies attackers by what they can reach and by what they can do. An adversary may have access only to the media path, only to the signaling path, or to both. An attacker confined to the signaling path, with no access to media at all, is not considered in this document.

From that, the RFC derives seven robustness classes, listed from easiest to compromise to hardest. The weakest are no-signaling-passive-media and no-signaling-active-media, where access to the media path alone is enough to reveal the content. The middle classes need a passive or an active attack on the signaling path as well. The strongest is active-signaling-active-media-detect: an attacker must be active on both paths, and the attack is detectable from the protocol messages exchanged between the endpoints.

The RFC works through examples. Unencrypted RTP falls in the weakest class. SDP Security Descriptions, when protected by TLS as they commonly are, sit in passive-signaling-passive-media, because an attacker who controls a SIP proxy can learn the key from the signaling message and then decrypt the media with it. DTLS-SRTP with a public-key cipher suite, self-signed certificates and no SIP Identity falls in active-signaling-active-media; adding SIP Identity and SIP Connected Identity moves it into the strongest class, provided the path to the authenticator and verifier is secured as those documents require. The same protocol can therefore land in different classes depending on the mode it runs in, and other protocols can reach the same result by adding functions outside the on-the-wire key management itself.

Because of this, the RFC states that the ultimate security requirement is that a media security negotiation protocol have a mode of operation that reaches the strongest class. Requirement R-ACT-ACT says exactly that, with the note that failing to meet it indicates the protocol cannot provide secure end-to-end media.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sorts attack situations from weakest to strongest. The best one needs an attacker to change both the call setup and the media, and lets the two ends notice that it happened.

sections.title: Call Scenarios That Shape the Requirements
sections.content:
Most of the requirements in this RFC come from ordinary call behaviour rather than from cryptography.

Clipping. Under the SDP offer/answer model, the offerer must be prepared to receive media for any receive-only stream described in its offer. With SRTP it also needs the key for that media, and if the key has not arrived the media cannot be played, which the RFC calls clipping. A provisional SIP response such as 183 (session progress) is useful, because it can carry the answerer's key early, but 183 messages are not reliable unless both endpoints support Provisional Response ACKnowledgement, use TCP across all SIP proxies, implement Security Preconditions, or both ends implement ICE with the answerer using ICE's reliable provisional response mechanism. None of those techniques had wide deployment, and there was industry reluctance to require them. The RFC also notes that sometimes the offerer must send media first to open firewall holes or NAT bindings, so even a solution that delivers the key before the SDP answer will not help in that case.

Retargeting and forking. A retarget is a request sent to one AOR but delivered to another, as with call forwarding: Alice invites Bob, Bob replies with a redirect to Carol, and the proxy sends the original INVITE to Carol. Forking is the delivery of one request to several locations, for example when a desk phone, a PC client and a mobile handset are all registered under the same AOR. The caller can neither anticipate nor prevent either condition, and SIP Identity can only identify the calling party, so it is hard to tell a legitimate forwarding from an attacker who rewrites the signaling. The security rule that follows is that only the endpoint that answers the call should learn the SRTP keys.

SIP adds one more wrinkle. When a forked request is rejected, only one final error response reaches the sender, chosen by the forking proxy. A rejection that says the keying information was refused, and carries the far end's credentials, may never reach the sender at all. The RFC calls this the Heterogeneous Error Response Forking Problem, cites RFC 3326, and says a media security system should function even when it happens.

Recording and transcoding. Some businesses, such as stock brokerages, banks and catalogue call centres, must record calls. Media recording is typically done by an intermediate device that has to see decrypted media, so the endpoint within the organisation has to be informed and has to cooperate with it. A network transcoder built the usual way looks exactly like a man-in-the-middle attack once the media is end-to-end secured, and the key management system prevents its use; it can still be built with the cooperation and approval of the endpoint.

Other scenarios. A PSTN gateway has to be able to terminate media security, which means the protection is not truly end-to-end on that leg. Some devices lack the processing power for a public key or Diffie-Hellman operation on every call; in one case such an operation can take a second or two, so reusing an earlier security context is useful, though storing keys across sessions interferes with perfect forward secrecy. A key management protocol must not require end-users to obtain credentials from a third-party trust anchor, so that people with no prior association can authenticate each other. Devices signalled with protocols other than SIP, or with a different key management system, are a further case; interworking them by decrypting and re-encrypting in the middle is always possible but undesirable, because it raises cost and enlarges the attack surface.
sections.plainLanguage: Real calls complicate things. A call can be forwarded to someone else, several phones can ring at once, sound can arrive before the answer, and a recorder may have to listen in. Each case changes what the key exchange has to do.

sections.title: The Requirement List
sections.content:
Section 5 splits the requirements three ways. The first group concerns the key management protocol itself. It must support forking and retargeting securely, so that endpoints which did not answer the call never learn the SRTP keys in either direction, and it must be able to create distinct, independent cryptographic contexts for each endpoint of a forked session. It must keep working when a rejection of the key information never reaches the sender. It should avoid clipping media before the SDP answer without requiring Security Preconditions. If the negotiation travels over the media path, on the same UDP or TCP ports as the media packets, its packets must not pass the RTP validity check defined in Appendix A.1 of RFC 3550, so that they can be told apart from RTP. It should associate key management messages with the signaling traffic that started the session and with the protected media, so that a device is not asked to do expensive Diffie-Hellman or public key work for parties it never called: the RFC's example is a Diffie-Hellman keying technique with security preconditions that forks to 20 endpoints, where the caller would otherwise have to compute 20 Diffie-Hellman secrets and validate 20 signatures. It must let a SIP user agent negotiate media security parameters for each individual session without causing a two-time pad, and it must support termination of media security in a PSTN gateway.

The second group covers security. The protocol must support perfect forward secrecy, must not introduce any new significant denial-of-service exposure by making endpoints perform CPU-intensive operations they cannot validate or authorise, and must be able to offer additional SRTP cipher suites without significant computational expense. It must protect cipher suite negotiation against downgrading attacks, must bind the media security keys cryptographically to an endpoint identity, and must have modes that defeat a passive adversary on the media path, a passive adversary on the signaling path, and an attacker confined to either one. It must offer a mode with active-signaling-active-media-detect robustness, and it must provide crypto agility, the ability to update cryptographic algorithms without substantial disruption to deployed implementations.

The third group sits outside the key management protocol and may be met elsewhere in the system. A solution must be described for mixed calls where some endpoints cannot use SRTP, for keys negotiated over other call signaling protocols such as Jabber, SIP, H.323 or the Media Gateway Control Protocol, for recording of decrypted media, for intermediate transcoders that terminate or process media, and for receiving plain RTP until SRTP has been negotiated with the answerer, after which SRTP is preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC groups its requirements into three piles: what the key exchange must handle, what it must defend against, and what the wider phone system has to sort out on its own.

sections.title: Existing Keying Mechanisms and How They Compare
sections.content:
Appendix A sorts the keying mechanisms by where the keys travel: the signaling path, the media path, or both. It notes two advantages of SRTP over other end-to-end encryption mechanisms such as IPsec: SRTP is bandwidth efficient, which matters where access bandwidth is limited or expensive, and SRTP retains the RTP header, which matters for troubleshooting packet loss, delay and jitter. It also notes that the media path is generally faster than the SIP signaling path, because the signaling path has proxies parsing and routing SIP messages, so the media path is useful for exchanging several messages to establish SRTP keys.

The appendix then compares the mechanisms against the call scenarios and the security criteria. The pattern that emerges is clear. Mechanisms where each endpoint works out its own key, such as MIKEY-DHSIGN, MIKEY-DHHMAC, SDP-DH, ZRTP and DTLS-SRTP, achieve secure forking and secure retargeting, because each forked endpoint negotiates unique keys with the offerer. Mechanisms that send a ready-made key, such as MIKEY-NULL, MIKEY-PSK, MIKEY-RSA and SDP Security Descriptions, do not: every branch of the fork, and every target of a retarget, sees the offerer's and answerer's keys. On perfect forward secrecy, MIKEY-DHSIGN, MIKEY-DHHMAC, SDP-DH and ZRTP provide it, DTLS-SRTP provides it when the negotiated cipher suite uses ephemeral keys, and MIKEY-PSK, MIKEY-RSA, MIKEY-RSA-R and EKT do not.

On cost, the mechanisms differ sharply. MIKEY-NULL, MIKEY-PSK and SDP Security Descriptions with SIPS add no significant computational expense, and ZRTP and DTLS-SRTP add none at all in the offer, because the ZRTP offer contains nothing about ZRTP and the DTLS-SRTP offer contains only a fingerprint of a certificate. The Diffie-Hellman based mechanisms pay for one operation per offered crypto suite. Because the offer has to list every combination of key exchange mechanism, SRTP cryptographic suite and SRTP hash function, the RFC asks that the offerer's CPU impact stay fixed so that offering more algorithms costs nothing extra.

Appendix B is out of scope: the compromise of an endpoint that already has access to decrypted media, such as a SIP user agent, transcoder or recorder, by privilege escalation, a virus or a trojan horse. It also records that the consensus on the working group's mailing list was to concentrate on unicast, point-to-point sessions, so no requirements are stated for shared key conferencing.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix compares the key exchange methods that existed in 2009. The ones where each phone works out its own key are safer when a call rings several phones, but they cost more computing time. The ones that send a ready-made key are cheaper but hand that key to every phone that rings.

items.title: no-signaling-passive-media
items.text: Access to the media path alone is enough to reveal the media content.

items.title: no-signaling-active-media
items.text: Active access to the media path alone is enough to reveal the media content.

items.title: passive-signaling-passive-media
items.text: A passive attack on both the signaling and the media path is needed.

items.title: passive-signaling-active-media
items.text: A passive signaling attack and an active media path attack are needed.

items.title: active-signaling-passive-media
items.text: An active signaling attack and a passive media path attack are needed.

items.title: active-signaling-active-media
items.text: Active attacks on both the signaling and the media path are needed.

items.title: active-signaling-active-media-detect
items.text: Active attacks on both paths are needed, and the endpoints can detect the attack.
